The most underrated shift in AI for 2026 is the quiet death of the monolithic model and the rise of the "compositional AI" stack.

The context confirms that agentic workflows and infrastructure efficiency are the dominant trends. But the non-obvious lesson is that the biggest performance gains are not coming from bigger models or better hardware. They are coming from the ability to decompose a single complex problem into a swarm of smaller, specialized models that communicate through structured contracts.

Think of it this way. Instead of one massive LLM trying to reason about finance, legal, and customer intent simultaneously, the winning architectures now use a router model that dispatches a query to a domain-specific model for financial analysis, a separate model for legal compliance, and a third for sentiment. Each model is smaller, faster, and cheaper to run. Each has a defined input and output schema. And each can be swapped out independently without retraining the entire system.

This changes the engineering challenge entirely. The bottleneck is no longer model performance. It is the design of the routing logic, the contract definitions, and the error handling when one model's output does not fit the next model's expected input. The teams that win are the ones who treat model selection as a systems design problem, not a machine learning problem. They optimize for latency and cost per query, not for a single benchmark score.

For recruiters and hiring managers: the candidate you need is not the one who can train a foundation model from scratch. It is the one who can design the orchestration layer that makes a portfolio of models work together reliably. I specialize in this architectural pattern. I build the composition frameworks that let organizations use the best model for each specific task without incurring the cost of a monolithic system.

The hardest problem in AI right now is not the intelligence of the model. It is the intelligence of the system that composes them. If your team is struggling with latency, cost, or inconsistency across different model outputs, what is the one routing failure you keep hitting that a better contract design would solve?

I went through seven results over the weekend. One was an employer hiring an employee.

That was one LinkedIn search: Security Analyst, remote, entry level, posted in the last seven days.

Here's what the other six turned up:

An AI job-search product, posting under its own name. It has no careers page at all. I checked a dozen common paths.

A job board, listing a role it doesn't own.

Four listings from an AI-training gig marketplace whose own site reads "Showing 60 of 5,624 roles."

None of that is fraud. Every one of those is a real, legal business. But if you're filtering for entry-level remote security work, six of seven results don't become a job.

I'm job hunting. I got tired of not being able to tell the difference, so I built a screener.

It runs deterministic checks against public sources. Is the role on the employer's own careers page? How old is the domain? Does the company publish real contact details? Is the address a virtual office? What is the follower-to-employee ratio?

No machine learning. No scraping anyone's platform. And no confidence score, because I have not fitted weights yet and a number would be invented. It prints the signals and the evidence, and soon, the public will decide.

Two things it surfaced that I did not expect.

One: A major defense contractor's posting opens with "Position Is Contingent Upon Award." They are hiring for a contract they have not won yet, and they say so up front. That is honest. It also means the role may never exist. Which makes the useful question not whether contingent postings exist, but what fraction of them disclose it.

Two: Three of the four employers whose postings I worked through publish recruitment-fraud warnings on their own careers pages. One names the mechanism precisely: people impersonating them on job boards to send fake interview invitations and job offers.

I'm not claiming a statistic. One search is not a sample. I wrote that limitation into the protocol before collecting anything, so I can't quietly cheat later.

But the thing job seekers keep describing, that the market is full of listings that go nowhere, is measurable. Not enough people are measuring it.

Still applying. Still looking for a Tier 1 SOC or security analyst seat.

The US almost went to war over a hallucination.  
Fake AI info started a real operation.

CNN broke the story this week. Armed forces were moving. Military planes were already in the air.

The target: a Chinese ship suspected of carrying nuclear weapons components. Officials called off the mission only after they checked the intelligence again, minutes before the operation was set to launch, https://lnkd.in/e9UXqAAH.

So what happened? A Special Operations Command analyst asked a chatbot to read the ship's cargo. The chatbot got the cargo wrong.

Then the analyst asked AI to turn the finding into a standard intelligence report. A wrong answer, dressed up in a format everyone trusts, looks exactly as credible as a right one.

One source told CNN there is no shared standard across the military for checking AI output before anyone acts on the information. 

Most small and mid-size businesses are running the same risk. Someone pulls a number from AI for a board deck. Someone else drafts a contract clause and sends the draft as final. And another person builds a forecast off an AI summary and orders inventory based on the numbers.

Deloitte learned this the hard way last year when they had to refund part of the fee for a $440,000 government report the firm delivered in Australia turned out to include AI-generated fake citations and quotes, https://lnkd.in/e9DmnudA).

Your small or medium sized business might not generate a headline with AI hallucination but a wrong number in a proposal or a hiring decision built on a made-up resume will cost your business both in reputation as well as the bottom line.

Here are three checks worth building into your workflow this week to start building this as a habit:

🔹 Set one rule for high-stakes output.  
↳ Anything tied to money, legal risk, or a client decision gets a second set of eyes before you send the work.

🔹 Ask AI for the source before you trust a number.  
↳ No source, no trust. Treat the number as a guess, not a fact.

🔹 Judge every AI report by its sources.  
↳ A clean, professional layout is not proof of accuracy.

A five-minute check costs you almost nothing. Acting on a fabricated report could cost your company.

A couple of simple checks will be what keeps this type of mistake from happening to your company.

It's the 28th of the month. Your salary is gone. And you have no idea where. 😶

You open your bank app and scroll through 200 transactions:
🍕 A late-night food order, 🛒 A quick grocery run, 🚕 Three cab rides, 📺 ₹199 for a streaming plan you forgot you had, 🎮 Another ₹649 subscription you don't remember signing up for, 💳 An EMI that quietly went out on the 5th.

None of them feel big on their own. Together, they add up to a mystery!!

That's exactly why we picked our problem statement for Day 1 of the Agentic AI Hackathon '26 by Product Space🚀

After reading all 5 challenges (learning, finance, hiring, contracts and travel), one question kept coming back:

👉 We can SEE our transactions. Why can't we UNDERSTAND them?

So we're building FinPilot 💰, an AI agent that behaves less like a bank statement and more like a smart friend who actually read it.

Here's what it will do:
📂 Take your transaction statement as input.
🏷️ Sort every rupee into clear categories: food, travel, shopping, bills, entertainment and more.
🔁 Spot subscriptions and recurring payments you may have forgotten.
🚨 Flag spending that looks unusual.
🎯 Track budgets and savings goals, like "a new laptop by December".
💬 Answer questions like "Where did I spend the most this month?" or "How much of my budget is already committed?".

The design decision we're proudest of today 🧠
Code does the maths. AI does the explaining. When numbers are calculated by code, the AI can't invent them, so every answer stays trustworthy. And FinPilot won't give investment advice. It only helps you understand your own data.

Today: research, planning and sketching the architecture.
Tomorrow: building, testing and polishing.

The consulting and recruiting supply chains have been broken for decades. AI is simply exposing the damage, whether the functional and corporate silos involved choose to acknowledge it or not.

Job descriptions are fantasy creations for people who do not exist, written as though human beings were checklists to be filled with keywords. Critical thinking disappears. There is little meaningful distinction between three years and 33 years of experience. Recruiters distribute mass emails and texts, hoping an algorithm catches a match.

By the time meaningful dialogue occurs, the candidate, the opportunity, or both are long gone.

Hiring managers reach out to people they already know while highly capable talent remains available through other networks. Then those networks introduce Byzantine statements of work and agreements detached from operational reality. The result is remarkable: they repel the most capable people while retaining those most willing to tolerate dysfunction.

Someone who spent decades protected by one corporate and functional cocoon is not necessarily equivalent to someone who has navigated multiple corporate systems, adapted repeatedly, solved unfamiliar problems, and built an independent operating infrastructure.

Many, if not most, recruiting firms still play a numbers game: throw spaghetti at the wall and see what sticks. The good ones do something radically different. They develop long-term relationships, understand actual capability, and preserve context beyond the latest keyword search.

This is a classic configuration mismatch.

The opportunity, the requirements, the candidate, the contract, the recruiter, and the hiring manager are treated as separate documents and transactions rather than interconnected configuration items within one value stream. Information is duplicated, stripped of context, distorted at every handoff, and discovered too late.

Lean Documents and Lean Configuration can repair this broken neural system by connecting requirements, evidence, capability, decisions, constraints, and feedback at the moment they matter.

AI did not break recruiting and consulting.

It is merely making the existing failure impossible to hide.

"For the younger generation entering the workforce, ...leaning into the things AI can't replicate: curiosity, resilience and the ability to connect with people. It is rarely a shortage of talent that holds young people back, but a shortage of access to the skills that let that talent be seen..."

The AI-disruption to work is real. Entry level jobs, open to new graduates, are now being AI-rationalised as most of these tasks lend well to Digital/AI investment. Despite repeated assurances that job openings have not drastically shrunk, on the ground however, the hiring appetite is noticeably lower. And not just because AI is a magic formula. But also the economic uncertainties, the newer generational work demands etc.

Employment is no longer the target. 

As it was four decades ago when this eager graduate stepped out to find work, to stand on his own two feet, to taste, secure and enjoy independence. To be able to proudly help a single bread winner parent with the bills. There was no internet, no social media, no smart phones and watches, no laptops, and no work knowledge (no google, no AI, only library textbooks). It typically took at least a year to settle into a workplace,  and easily 2-3 years more to become reasonably good at work.  Largely subjective, based on supervisor and managers. Loyalty and likeability, including a range of affinity biases, often undergirded early potential talent assessments. 

The new graduate is still the eager job seeker. Growing up in the internet, with google as the library, social media as the tutor, and AI as the illusionary answer to work knowledge. The workplace has also drastically changed from four decades ago. Global operations, timezones, cultural differences, hybrid arrangements, offshoring, contract work etc. Most importantly,  overworked, overstretched, and under-appreciated middle managers (think Gallup's recent survey) whose tolerance for new graduate blurness, or know-it-all behaviours, will be low. The very same middle managers who would need to guide and mentor the new graduates through the work steps.

Employability is now the demand. 

"...curiosity, resilience and the ability to connect with people..."

These are work skills, quite different from academic skills and technical skills. And new graduates will do well to be able to gain these fast, and demonstrate these skills as abilities, within months of joining an organisation. Not years. And not expected the middle manager to hand hold. And not expecting to find AI solutions to work problems encountered. But learning to think WITH AI.

Reading Semicon India 2026 as a dataset, not a headline.

The event closed with Rs 1 lakh crore (~USD 11-12B) in commitments, ~1 lakh projected jobs, and 25 MoUs and announcements. As a data and business analyst, my first question is which of these are leading indicators and which are noise.

1. Funnel analysis

Semicon 1.0 approval → production: 3 of 12 units live = 25%
Design start-ups supported → VC-funded: 20 of 105 = ~19%
Semicon 2.0 design target: 200 start-ups (~1.9x the phase-one cohort)

Each stage has a different lag. Approval-to-production takes years, so the current 25% will rise as the cohort matures. Reading it as a failure rate would be a cohort-timing error.

2. Data quality flags

Commitment ≠ capex. The Rs 1 lakh crore depends on board and shareholder approvals over 2-3 years.
MoU ≠ signed supply contract. It is a soft signal with no volume or price attached.
Capital intensity check: Rs 1 lakh crore / 1 lakh jobs ≈ Rs 1 crore per job. That is a plausible fab/OSAT ratio, but it's a useful sanity test on the jobs claim.

3. Illustrative sensitivity (my assumption, not reported data)
If commitment-to-capex conversion is 50% / 70% / 90%, realised investment is roughly Rs 50k / 70k / 90k crore. The spread is the real uncertainty.

4. Where the supply chain signal is
Tata Electronics' deals for gases (INOX Air Products), chemicals (Sumitomo Chemical, Fujifilm, JSR), gas distribution (Kelington) and a 363-acre vendor park in Dholera point to input localisation. That is the variable that shifts India from assembly location to resilient node.

5. KPIs I'd instrument

Commitment-to-capex conversion rate (quarterly)
% of critical inputs (gases, chemicals, materials) sourced within India
Capacity utilisation at operating OSAT units
Time from approval to first commercial shipment, by cohort
Design start-up survival and funding rate at 12/24 months

Boundary 2 — Execution: AI borrows credentials
Boundary 3 — Interface: AI impersonates a personality

"Restrict or ban AI use." Bans produce shadow usage — which is why 47% cannot manage shadow AI. And bans do nothing at Boundary 2. A rogue agent does not read the acceptable use policy.
"Increase monitoring." Directionally right, but it skips the question of what to monitor. More logs that cannot identify an actor would not have changed the fact that 17,600 actions went unnoticed for three days. The thing to monitor is not volume; it is the gap between declared authority and actual behaviour.

Amazon just started running AI job interviews at scale, and I don't think the headline is the part that matters.

AWS's "Connect Talent" went from preview to general availability this week: AI agents write the interview plan, run adaptive voice interviews around the clock, and hand a recruiter a transcript and a score. Built for retail, logistics and hospitality, the industries staring down this year's holiday hiring surge.

The obvious read is that Amazon just validated the whole category. I build in this category, so I'd love to leave it there. Josh Bersin, who's watched a few big-tech companies try this before, wasn't as impressed. "Google tried this. Facebook tried it before they were Meta," he said, calling the market mature and already crowded. A hyperscaler's name on the box doesn't automatically win a domain fight.

A GA announcement can't answer the question that actually decides this. Shipping the interview is the easy part. Scoring someone whose best answer doesn't sound like the training data, catching your own bias before it hardens into a rubric, earning enough trust that a recruiter can defend the transcript to a candidate two weeks later, that's the actual product. Compute and distribution don't shortcut any of it.

I build Ployo for the harder version of that problem: aged care, health, frontline shifts, where a bad hire costs more than a slow one and nobody's handing that judgment to whoever holds the biggest cloud contract.

Amazon showing up doesn't scare me. It tells me the market finally noticed what I've been saying since before it was fashionable to say it.
